newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's ethnic Turks join anti-Socialist unrest.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's ethnic Turks join anti-Socialist unrest.

text.p: Some 2,000 protesters gathered in this ethnic Turkish region of southern Bulgaria on Saturday to add their voice to nationwide demands for the government of former communists to quit.

Bulgaria's 800,000 Turks have a special grudge against the ruling Socialists, recalling efforts to make them change their names to Bulgarian ones and discourage Islam in the last years of communist dictatorship which forced many to flee to Turkey.

But the rally in cold and fog in the town of Kardzhali was fired less by ethnic tensions than the anger, shared by most Bulgarians, at poverty deepened by inflation of more than 300 percent and widely blamed on Socialist mismanagement.

"We don't know what to do," said Ahmed Sargun, a retired miner. "My pension is only enough to buy 100 loaves of bread a month. My son fled Bulgaria to seek a better job in Turkey. I hope he is doing better."

Protesters arrived in Kardzhali by bus from seven small towns and villages nearby, carrying placards reading "Communists go in peace", "1997 -- end of communism in Bulgaria", "Red trash" and "Death to the (Socialist) BSP".
There was no hint of violence and small groups of police chatted with demonstrators.
"I was a miner but my pension is 4,000 levs ($6) a month," said elderly Azis Usein Delimehmedov.
"These people (the Socialists) up there do not think of the people but how to plunder Bulgaria. If I were younger and had anywhere to go I would not stay a day longer."

Dimana Hristova, a teacher and one of the ethnic Bulgarians outnumbered by up to four to one in the Kardzhali region, joined the protest which echoed the dozens held daily across the country for the last two weeks.
"Not only Turks but also Bulgarians have fled the region to Turkey looking for better jobs. They have chased all of us away," she said.
The ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF), has 15 seats in Bulgaria's 240-seat national parliament.
But protesters blamed past ethnic tensions on policies of the ex-communist ruling Socialists.
"The communists are strong here and always play the nationalist card," said Elena Dimitorova, an ethnic Bulgarian teacher.

"Now they have started a campaign to separate the local authorities of the town of Kardzhali from surrounding villages so that, in the next local election, the mayor will not be an ethnic Turk but a Bulgarian."
"There is no such thing as Bulgarians against Turks or vice versa," added Karsimira Kamenova, director of a child care centre. "We drink our coffee and liquor together."
The opposition accuses the ruling party, who won power in free elections in 1994, of both incompetence and corruption.

Free market reforms of the kind introduced in most east European countries have barely begun and protesters point to dubious links between Socialist politicians and powerful business groups in the still mainly state-controlled economy.
"I have six children but don't know whom to feed first," said Mehmed Mumun Ahmed, 52, an ethnic Turk from a village nearby. "Jobs can't be found anywhere."
